region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita', eBook #8299

summary.en: Directed by an old man to a palace guarded by monkeys — whom he must feed his bread before entering — Don Juan is married on the spot to Chonguita, the big monkey's daughter. Hauled home in shame, she outdoes her human sisters-in-law at every task set by the king hoping to destroy her: the embroidered coat, the cap, the prettiest picture. When Don Juan, furious that she insists he dance with her, hurls her against the wall, the hall darkens and Chonguita is transformed into a beautiful woman.
summary.zh: 老人指路，令唐·胡安以麵包餵過守宮猴群方可入內——他當場與大猴之女瓊桂塔成婚。羞愧還鄉，國王屢設難題欲除猴媳；繡衣、繡帽、繪畫，猴妻樣樣奪魁。慶典之上，唐·胡安被妻子逼舞，怒將她擲向牆壁——大廳驟暗復明，瓊桂塔化為絕色佳人。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from an Ejercito narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Monkey-bride cycle; Fansler compares the Greek monkey-wife of Von Hahn No. 67 and Grimm's Three Feathers family, and notes the wall-hurling disenchantment matches Grimm's frog-prince.

passages.text: There was a king who had three sons, named Pedro, Diego, and Juan. One day the king ordered these three gentlemen to set out from the kingdom and seek their fortunes; they took different directions, but before they separated they agreed to meet in a certain place in the forest. After walking for many days, Don Juan met an old man on the road, who gave him bread and told him to go to a palace a mile away: 'But as you enter the gate, you must divide the bread which I have given you among the monkeys which are guarding the gate to the palace; otherwise you will not be able to enter.' Don Juan took the bread, and when he reached the palace he did as the old man had advised him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After entering the gate he saw a big monkey, and frightened at the sight of the animal he was about to run away — when the animal called to him and said, 'Don Juan, I know that your purpose in coming here was to find your fortune; and at this very moment my daughter Chonguita will marry you.' The archbishop of the monkeys was called, and Don Juan and Chonguita were married without delay. A few days afterwards Don Juan asked permission from his wife to go to the place where he and his brothers had agreed to meet; when Chonguita's mother heard that he was going away she said, 'If you are going away, take Chonguita with you.' Although Don Juan was ashamed to go with Chonguita because she was a monkey, he was forced to take her, and they set out together. When Don Juan met his two brothers and their beautiful wives at the appointed place, he could not say a word — 'Here she is... Behind me,' he sadly replied to their questions, and at Don Pedro's exclamation, 'What happened to you? Did you lose your head?' he could say nothing but 'Let us go home! Our father must be waiting for us.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Upon learning that one of his sons had married a monkey, the king fainted; after recovering his senses he said to himself, 'This misfortune is God's will. I must therefore bear it with patience,' and assigned a house to each couple. But the more he thought of it, the greater appeared the disgrace his youngest son had brought on the family, and one day he called his three sons together: 'Tell your wives that I want each one of them to make me an embroidered coat. The one who falls to do this within three days will be put to death.' He issued this order in the hope that Chonguita would be put to death, because he thought she would not be able to make the coat — but on the third day his daughters-in-law presented the coats, and the one embroidered by Chonguita was the prettiest of all. Still anxious to get rid of the monkey-wife, the king next ordered his daughters-in-law to embroider a cap for him in two days, under penalty of death; the caps were all done on time. At last, thinking of no other way, the king summoned his three daughters-in-law: 'The husband of the one who shall be able to draw the prettiest picture on the walls of my chamber within three days shall succeed me on the throne.' At the end of the three days, when the king went to inspect the pictures, he found that Chonguita's was by far the prettiest, and so Don Juan was crowned king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A great feast was held in the palace in honor of the new king. In the midst of the festivities Don Juan became very angry with his wife for insisting that he dance with her, and he hurled her against the wall. At this brutal action the hall suddenly became dark; but after a while it became bright again, and Chonguita had been transformed into a beautiful woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省巴蘭彥（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock', eBook #8299

summary.en: Proud Pio wagers his life against Ludovico's that he can learn the secrets of the recluse Clotilde in fifteen days; a bribed chaperon sells him one of the three golden locks under his wife's left armpit. Condemning her as faithless, Ludovico awaits the scaffold — until Clotilde arrives in her jeweled golden slipper, accuses Pio before the king of stealing 'my other slipper which looks like this one,' and his denial — 'I don't even know her. This is the first time I have ever seen her' — convicts him of the lie about her secrets. Pio is hanged in Ludovico's place, and the treacherous old woman ends her days in a dungeon.
summary.zh: 狂徒皮奧以性命打賭：十五日內必探得隱居的克洛蒂爾德的秘密。受賄的老侍婢賣給他一縷『左腋下三縷金髮』。盧多維科見金髮，信妻不貞，靜待極刑。刑前片刻，克洛蒂爾德穿著鑲寶金鞋趕到，當眾指控皮奧『偷了我另一隻一模一樣的金鞋』；皮奧矢口『從未見過她』——恰恰證明他所謂的秘密純屬謊言。皮奧代盧多維科受絞，賣主的老婆子終老地牢。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (tale from Balayan); archival record. Chastity-wager cycle; Fansler traces the family from the Roman de Guillaume de Dole through Boccaccio Decameron 2:9 and Shakespeare's Cymbeline, and parallels the Tagalog corridos Duke Almanzor and Rodolfo.

passages.text: Long ago there lived in a distant kingdom an influential noble named Ludovico, who vastly increased his wealth by his marriage to a rich heiress called Clotilde. During the first ten years of their union she had never peeped out of her window or stirred out of her room: she only walked to the door of her chamber to bid farewell to her husband, and to meet him with a tender embrace when he returned. Nobody else but Ludovico and her chaperon could see or talk with her; she spent her time in voluntary seclusion, not in the luxuries of the court or the gaieties of society, but in embroidery, knitting, and in the unnecessary embellishment of her extremely lovely person.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the king's banquet in one of the principal frontier cities, the garrulous Pio, a bold, sharp-tongued rich youth, ridiculed the noble constancy of the fair Clotilde. 'I will bet you anything you want to bet, that you cannot learn the secrets of my wife in fifteen days,' said Ludovico, his face flushed with wrath. 'All right,' said Pio, exasperated by Ludovico's boast. 'The loser shall be hanged. I will bet my life that I'll know the secrets of your wife within fifteen days.' The terms of the contract were carefully written down, solemnly ratified by the king, and signed by the two contestants and by the other high-born gentlemen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pio set out the next day for Ludovico's home town, and by his persuasive language and the magnetic touch of his hands he easily insinuated himself into the confidence of the gray-haired chaperon, then dropping a piece of gold on her palm: 'Will you tell me the secrets of your mistress?' The brilliant coin proved too great a temptation for her. 'Clotilde has three golden locks of hair under her left armpit. I know this fact, because I bathe her every day.' A second gold-piece bought her promise of the lock itself, and early the next morning, while bathing Clotilde as usual, she pulled out one of the golden locks — 'Aray! What's the matter with you?' — 'Never mind, never mind! This is the only reward I want for my many faithful services to you.' Ignorant of the treasonable intrigues of her chaperon, Clotilde said nothing more, and the old woman was amply rewarded with a purse of gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ludovico was struck aghast at the sight of the golden lock, and at once wrote to his wife: 'I have spent ten years of my life in perfect happiness with you... But now everything is hopeless. My life shall be ended by violence, because of your faithlessness. We shall see each other no more. Receive the sad farewell of your Ludovico.' When Clotilde read this letter she swooned; coming to her senses, she read again the opprobrious word 'faithlessness' in her husband's handwriting, not knowing what act of disloyalty she had committed. At last a thought came to her mind: she sent for the best goldsmith in town and told him to make her a gold slipper adorned with precious stones; then she put on her best clothes and the precious slipper and with all possible expedition set out for Ludovico, arriving in the city just a few minutes before the execution. The turbulent persons gathered in the public square were awed by the loveliness and magnificent attire of Clotilde; when she reached the king and had heard all the details of Ludovico's case, she turned and pointed toward Pio: 'That man has stolen my other slipper which looks like this one I am wearing.' 'I have not committed any crime against her,' said Pio angrily. 'I don't even know her. This is the first time I have ever seen her.' 'Sir, why, then, did you tell his Majesty and other persons that you have discovered my secrets? I am the wife of Ludovico, whose life you have threatened to end by your deceit. I know now by what means you got possession of my golden lock.' Clotilde's statement sealed Pio's fate: he was hanged in place of Ludovico, who deeply regretted having doubted his faithful wife — and the old woman who preferred the gold of an impostor to the kindness of a virtuous woman was sentenced to spend the remainder of her life in a damp, dreary dungeon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.
